title: How to Detect a Hidden Camera Using Your Phone (Free Methods That Actually Work in 2026)
excerpt: Your smartphone can detect most hidden cameras for free — if you use the right technique. Here's what actually works, what doesn't, and the one method that catches cameras other tools miss.
body:
Does Your Phone Actually Detect Hidden Cameras?

Sort of — and understanding when it works and when it doesn't will save you from relying on a method that fails when you need it most.

Your phone can detect hidden cameras in specific situations: WiFi-connected cameras (via network scanning), infrared-emitting cameras (via your phone camera's IR sensitivity), and cameras with reflective lenses (via flashlight sweep). What your phone cannot reliably detect: wired cameras not connected to WiFi, cameras in faraday-shielded housings, and cameras with IR-cut filters that block the IR signature.

With that context set, here are the methods that genuinely work.

Method 1: Infrared Detection With Your Phone Camera

Many hidden cameras emit infrared light for night vision. Most phones can see infrared light — specifically, the front-facing camera on iPhones and many Android phones lacks the IR filter found on rear cameras. This means the front camera shows IR as visible light in a dark room.

How to test your phone first: Point a TV remote at your front camera and press a button. If you see a flashing light on screen (often pink or purple), your front camera detects IR. If the rear camera shows nothing but the front camera shows the flash, you've confirmed which camera to use for detection.

The scan:

  1. Turn off all lights and close curtains
  2. Open your camera app and switch to the front camera
  3. Slowly scan the room, especially toward suspected camera locations
  4. Look for any faint glow that isn't visible to the naked eye
  5. Common hidden camera locations: smoke detectors, alarm clocks, USB chargers, picture frames, air purifiers

Limitation: This only detects cameras with active IR illumination. Cameras with IR-cut filters (which engage in daytime) or cameras using other illumination methods won't be detected this way.

Method 2: WiFi Network Scan (Finds Most Modern Hidden Cameras)

The majority of hidden cameras sold in 2026 are WiFi-enabled. They connect to the property's network to transmit footage remotely. Scanning the same network reveals unfamiliar connected devices.

Use Fing (free app, iOS and Android):

  1. Connect your phone to the property's WiFi
  2. Download and open Fing
  3. Tap
• Review the device list — look for manufacturers you don't recognize or device names with

or surveillance-related brand names
  • Common camera brands to flag: Wyze, Reolink, Amcrest, Hikvision, Dahua, TP-Link, Eufy, Ezviz

    • False positives: Smart TVs, streaming sticks, gaming consoles, and the router itself will appear. Focus on devices whose manufacturer or device name suggests a camera.

    What this misses: Cameras with their own SIM card and cellular data, cameras on a separate network, and hardwired cameras with no wireless component.

    Method 3: Phone Flashlight Sweep (Finds Lens Reflections)

    Camera lenses create a distinctive retroreflection when a bright light source hits them at the right angle. In a dark room with your phone flashlight at full brightness, sweep slowly across all surfaces while looking for a small, bright dot — often with a slight color tint (blue, red, or greenish).

    This works regardless of whether the camera is WiFi-connected, IR-emitting, or even powered on. The lens itself creates the reflection.

    Best results: Very dark room, slowest possible scan speed, check from multiple angles for each suspect area. Camera lenses are small — the reflection is a 1-3mm bright point.

    Method 4: RF Detector Apps — Be Honest About These

    Most

apps in the App Store and Google Play are effectively useless or outright scams. They display fake signal readings to appear functional. Avoid any app that claims to detect cameras via magnetic field readings — camera lenses do not produce magnetic fields.

The only free phone method for RF detection is using a WiFi scanner to identify transmitting devices on the network — which is Method 2 above. There is no legitimate phone-based RF scanner app that works for detecting hidden cameras.

If you need RF detection, a dedicated hardware detector ($25-90) is necessary. The JMDHKK RF detector is the most reviewed budget option.

Method 5: Two-Mirror Test for Two-Way Mirrors

A one-way mirror (common in fitting rooms and interrogation rooms) looks like a regular mirror from one side but is transparent from the other — a camera could be behind it. The quick test: press your fingernail directly against the mirror surface.

In a genuine mirror, there will be a gap between your fingernail and its reflection. In a two-way mirror or a mirror with a gap behind it, your fingernail and the reflection will appear to touch with no gap. This is because real mirrors have a glass layer between your fingernail and the reflective surface.

Building a Complete Phone-Based Check

Combine all methods for the most thorough free check in under 10 minutes:

  1. Network scan with Fing immediately on arrival (2 minutes)
  2. Dark room flashlight sweep of bedroom and bathroom (3 minutes)
  3. IR scan with front camera in dark room (2 minutes)
  4. Two-mirror test on all mirrors in private areas (1 minute)
  5. Manual inspection of unusual or out-of-place objects (2 minutes)

This combination catches the vast majority of consumer-grade hidden cameras. Professional surveillance equipment designed to evade detection requires dedicated countermeasure hardware to find.

When Phone Methods Aren't Enough

If you're in a situation where you have specific reason to believe sophisticated surveillance is in place (corporate espionage, targeted harassment), phone methods are insufficient. Dedicated equipment — specifically a lens detector combined with an RF spectrum analyzer — is required. Some professional TSCM (Technical Surveillance Countermeasures) services sweep hotels and offices for fees starting around $200/hour.

For the vast majority of travelers and renters, the free phone methods above provide meaningful protection against consumer-grade hidden cameras that represent the actual threat in short-term rentals and budget hotels.

Summary: What Works and What Doesn't

Phone methods that work: WiFi network scan for connected cameras, IR detection via front camera for night-vision cameras, flashlight sweep for lens reflections, mirror test for two-way mirrors. Phone methods that don't work: magnetic sensor apps, fake RF detector apps, any app claiming to detect cameras through walls or without network access. For complete detection including non-transmitting local-storage cameras, a hardware lens detector ($30) is the most reliable addition to these free methods.
